About: Projectile Motion — Independent x and y

Source

Simulation
Projectile Motion — Independent x and y (live launch + vertical-twin race + range-vs-angle function plot, with a runnable counterfactual "coupled" model).
Concept
Horizontal and vertical projectile motions are independent: x(t) = v₀cosθ·t at constant velocity; y(t) = v₀sinθ·t − ½gt² under gravity alone (SI units, g = 9.81 m/s²).
Serves
Component decomposition of 2-D motion; R = v₀²sin2θ/g peaking at 45° (R_max = v₀²/g); complementary angles (30°/60°) give equal range. Kernel-verified anchors: 25 m/s @ 40° → R = 62.74 m, T = 3.28 s, H = 13.16 m; 30° vs 60° → 55.17 m = 55.17 m; 45° → 63.71 m.
Inquiry
Does the tie-line between the projectile and its vertical twin ever tilt as v₀ grows? Which velocity arrow changes in flight? Which angle maximizes range, and why do θ and 90°−θ land at the same spot but at different times?
Misconception
"Horizontal and vertical motions influence each other — a faster horizontal throw falls more slowly." Encoded as prediction choice ⓐ and as the runnable ⚠ Coupled model (a_y = −g·sinθ), falsified by contrast with the ✓ Independent model.

Launch a ball from the ground, set its speed and angle, and follow the arc it traces.

How would you like to begin?

Listen to the intro

Guided Inquiry

1 · One launch

Let’s meet our ball. Ball A leaves the ground at v₀ = 25 m/s and θ = 40° above the horizontal. You’ll see its velocity drawn in two pieces, a horizontal component and a vertical component, while gravity acts straight down with g = 9.81 m/s².

2 · The twin race

Now for a race. At the same instant, a second ball is thrown straight up with the same vertical speed v₀sinθ and no horizontal velocity at all. Which ball do you think reaches the ground first?

3 · Two angles, one speed

Let’s play with the angle instead. Two balls are launched at the same speed, one at 30° and one at 60°. How far from the launch point do you expect each one to land?

4 · The longest shot

Now take that one step further. 30° and 60° share a range, and so does every other pair of angles adding to 90°. So which single launch angle do you think sends the ball farthest?

5 · Where, and when

Time to watch it happen. Both balls are now launched at 25 m/s, one at 30° and one at 60°. Compare where each one lands — and then compare when each one lands. Notice anything?

6 · Doubling the launch speed

One last question. The launch angle is held fixed, and the launch speed v₀ is doubled. By what factor do you think the range changes?

Exact values for the current sliders (✓ model): T = 2v₀sinθ/g, H = (v₀sinθ)²/2g, R = v₀²sin2θ/g, with g = 9.81 m/s².

Horizontal: no horizontal force ⇒ constant velocity. Gravity never touches x.
Vertical: free fall. vₓ does not appear anywhere in y(t) — that absence is the independence.
Hang time and peak height come from the vertical component alone — the twin ball shares both exactly.
Range: constant vₓ times the vertical clock. Peaks at θ = 45° (sin2θ = 1 ⇒ Rmax = v₀²/g).
Complementary angles land at the same spot — 30° and 60° share R (55.17 m at v₀ = 25 m/s) but not T.
⚠ The falsified "coupled" model behind the myth: hang time independent of angle, flat throws never land. Runnable via the ⚠ button — and refuted by every real fall.

The Physics

Projectile motion · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim launches a ball from flat ground at the speed and angle you choose, draws its arc, and splits its velocity into a horizontal and a vertical part. Extra balls let you race launches against each other, which is how you find out what the arc really depends on.

What you'll learn

  • What the horizontal and vertical parts of the velocity each do during the flight.
  • What sets how long a ball stays in the air.
  • How the range depends on the launch angle.
  • How the range depends on the launch speed.
Ball A leaves the ground at speed v₀ and angle θ. Its launch velocity splits into a horizontal part (amber) and a vertical part (blue).

What's on screen

  • Ball A (amber ring): your launch. Its arrows show vₓ (amber) and vy (blue).
  • Launcher: the v₀ arrow at angle θ, split into its two parts.
  • Ball B (cyan): the twin, from ⇅ Twin ball.
  • Ball M (violet): the ball at 90° − θ, from ⧉ 90°−θ.
  • Previous trials: faint arcs of earlier launches.
  • Landing flags: each ball's flight time and range.
See itLaunch ball A at the current settings. Watch for: the landing flag, which shows the flight time and the range.

Fixed: g = 9.81 m/s², no air drag, and every ball is launched from and lands on the same flat ground.

03

Two motions share one clock

After launch the only force is gravity, and it points straight down. So the ball has no horizontal acceleration, and a constant downward acceleration g.

The opening launch, 25 m/s at 40°. The horizontal velocity never changes; the vertical one shrinks, vanishes at the top, then grows downward.
Horizontal: no force, so constant velocity.
Vertical: free fall. vₓ appears nowhere in y(t).
  • The two motions share only the time t. Neither one affects the other.
  • x grows steadily with t while y is quadratic in t, so the path is a parabola.
  • At the top only vy is zero. The ball still moves sideways at v₀ cos θ, and its acceleration is still g, downward.
See itLaunch ball A with its velocity arrows. Watch for: the amber arrow keeps the same length all flight, while the blue one shrinks to nothing at the top and then grows pointing down.
04

What sets the flight time

The flight time and the peak height come from the vertical motion alone:

Set by v₀ sin θ and g only.
  • Twin ball B starts with the same vertical speed v₀ sin θ as A, but no horizontal speed. Its y(t) is the same as A's, term by term.
  • So the two balls are at the same height at every instant, and land together. At 25 m/s and 40° both land after 3.28 s.
  • A's horizontal speed only carries it sideways. It does not keep A up any longer.
The twin race at the opening launch, with two same-height moments marked.
See itRace ball A against twin B. Watch for: the dashed line between the balls staying level ("same height"), and both landing flags showing the same time.
05

Range is drift times flight time

The ball drifts sideways at a steady v₀ cos θ for the whole flight time T, so the range is their product:

Valid for launch and landing at the same height.
v₀ θ

These sliders move the sim too.

  • Launch speed feeds both factors: double v₀ and the drift doubles and so does T. The range grows four times (R ∝ v₀²).
  • At 40°: 25 m/s gives 62.74 m, and 50 m/s gives 250.97 m.
See itLaunch at 40° with 25 m/s, then with 50 m/s. Watch for: the second ball lands four times as far, and the card shows both ranges side by side.
06

How the angle sets the range

The angle enters the range only through sin 2θ, and sin 2θ takes the same value for θ and 90° − θ:

  • At 25 m/s, 30° and 60° both land 55.17 m away. The steeper ball stays up longer (4.41 s against 2.55 s) but drifts more slowly, and the two effects cancel.
  • 45° pairs with itself, and there sin 2θ = 1 is largest: Rmax = v₀²/g, which is 63.71 m at 25 m/s.
Three angles at 25 m/s.
See itLaunch at 30° and 60° together. Watch for: both flags at the same range, with different flight times.
See itLaunch at 45° with 📈 Range vs angle open. Watch for: the amber marker sits at the top of the green curve.
07

Where it matters

  • Throwing events. Shot-putters release well below 45°, typically in the mid-30s. The shot leaves from about 2 m above the ground, and athletes can throw faster at flatter angles. Both break the sim's assumptions.
  • Air drag. For a fast, light ball such as a hit baseball, drag shortens the flight a lot and pulls the best angle below 45°. The sim leaves drag out so the two motions stay separate.
  • On the Moon, g = 1.62 m/s². Since R ∝ 1/g, the same 25 m/s throw at 45° would land about 386 m away, six times farther, after about 22 s in the air.
Go deeper: the shape of the path
  • Take t = x / (v₀ cos θ) from the horizontal motion and put it into y(t). The time drops out: y = x tan θ − g x² / (2 v₀² cos² θ).
  • This is a downward parabola in x. It starts with slope tan θ, peaks halfway along at x = R/2, and lands with slope −tan θ.
08

Summary

In one line. A projectile drifts sideways at constant speed while it falls freely, and its range is that drift speed times the flight time.

Key points

  • aₓ = 0 and ay = −g, so vₓ = v₀ cos θ never changes.
  • Flight time T = 2v₀ sin θ / g depends only on the vertical launch speed.
  • R = v₀² sin 2θ / g: angles θ and 90° − θ share a range, and 45° gives the most.
  • Doubling v₀ doubles T and quadruples R and H.

Common mix-ups

  • "A faster sideways throw stays up longer." vₓ does not appear in y(t), so the twin lands at the same moment.
  • "At the top the ball is at rest." Only vy is zero there. vₓ is unchanged, and the acceleration is still g.
  • "Double the speed, double the range." Drift and flight time both double, so the range quadruples.

Things to try on your own

  • Launch at 90° with the twin on, and compare the two balls.
  • Launch at 30° with 20 m/s, then 40 m/s, and compare the ranges.
  • At 25 m/s, find the two angles that both land 31.86 m away.
